posts.title: Test web agents against goals and paths
posts.promise: Run repeatable scenarios and review where a web agent succeeds or gets stuck.
posts.whatItIs: Senro is described by its maker as a platform for testing WebMCP tools, meaning tools a web page exposes for an AI agent. Its described tests include goal-oriented evaluations and trajectory evaluations across language models, and it can monitor production use. A small student version could store a few test goals, run them against a demo web tool, and save pass/fail results with the action path. Developers building agent-accessible web tools are a plausible paying customer; that customer and willingness to pay are hypotheses, not established by this source.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers or teams maintaining WebMCP tools may pay to catch regressions; the source does not establish paying customers.
loop: Load saved test goals for a demo WebMCP tool.
Run each goal through a selected model and tool.
Record the action sequence and final result.
Compare results with the expected outcome.
Alert a developer when a result changes or fails.
A person reviews failures and updates the test or tool.
posts.evidence: The Show HN author says Senro tests WebMCP tools with goal-oriented and trajectory evaluations across LLMs and monitors production use. The author also describes a free plan with stated monthly event and evaluation limits using the user's own API key; these are founder-provided claims.
posts.uncertainty: The source is a founder description, not independent validation. It does not show evaluation accuracy or customer demand. The student version would test a controlled demo; model variation can make results inconsistent, and a person should diagnose failures before changing a live tool.
first24Hours: Choose a public demo page with a harmless WebMCP tool and write five clear goals.
Build a script that runs each goal once and records tool actions and results.
Create a simple report that flags failed or changed outcomes for human review.

posts.title: Route visual feedback to a coding agent
posts.promise: Turn a marked-up staging page into an agent task with a reviewable status trail.
posts.whatItIs: CircleIt is described as a Chrome extension plus a Claude Code or Codex plugin. A teammate can mark an area on a page, explain the requested change, and send the screenshot, comment, and page metadata to a running coding agent. The source says the system matches the page address to a repository and reports status back in the sender's browser. A small student version could capture one staging page and open a proposed task for a developer's agent. Small product teams are a plausible customer, but that is a hypothesis. The loop handles intake and handoff; a human still needs to judge whether the requested change is correct and review code before release.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: small software teams that collect frequent website feedback may pay; no customer or payment evidence is given.
loop: A teammate opens a staging page and marks a visible issue.
Capture the screenshot, comment, page address, and relevant metadata.
Match the page address to a configured repository.
Send the feedback to the team's running coding agent after any required approval.
Show the sender the agent's status and response.
A developer reviews code changes and decides whether to merge.
posts.evidence: The Show HN author describes a Chrome extension and Claude Code/Codex plugin, screenshot and comment transfer to a running agent, address-based repository routing, status updates, and optional approval requirements for people or sites. The author reports a time improvement for their own small UI changes; this is an attributed personal claim.
posts.uncertainty: The workflow is based on the maker's account and does not independently establish reliability or adoption. For a student MVP, limit access to a test repository and staging site. Address matching can route incorrectly, and agent-generated changes need human review before deployment.
first24Hours: Create a disposable demo page and test repository with one visible UI issue.
Build a browser capture form for a marked region, comment, and page URL.
Route one captured report to a task queue and add a manual approval step before an agent receives it.

posts.title: Check whether docs work for AI agents
posts.promise: Scan a documentation URL for common access and format problems, then review a scorecard.
posts.whatItIs: Velu's agent-friendly documentation checker is described as scoring a documentation URL against the open Agent-Friendly Documentation Spec, using the spec's reference implementation called afdocs. The Show HN post names issues the spec is concerned with: pages rendered only in the browser, missing llms.txt or Markdown versions, soft 404 pages, and pages too large for an agent's context window. A beginner could build a small scheduled checker for one documentation site that records the score and lists detectable problems. Documentation teams are a plausible customer, but the source does not establish who pays. This is an audit and reporting loop, not an automatic documentation repair service.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: teams maintaining developer documentation may pay for recurring checks; the source does not establish customers or revenue.
loop: Read a configured documentation site URL.
Check pages for supported agent access and format signals.
Run the reference checker and save its score.
Compare the result with the previous scan.
Send a report when the score or detected issues change.
A documentation owner verifies findings and chooses any fix.
posts.evidence: The Show HN description says Velu's tool scores documentation URLs against the open Agent-Friendly Documentation Spec using its reference implementation, afdocs. The author identifies client-rendered pages, missing llms.txt or Markdown, soft 404s, and oversized pages as problems the spec addresses.
posts.uncertainty: This is a maker's description; the snapshot does not include an independent test or performance data. A student checker can only detect a limited set of public signals and may misclassify sites. A human should verify a finding before editing a documentation site.
first24Hours: Select a public documentation site and inspect the referenced open specification and checker interface.
Implement checks for one or two signals such as Markdown availability and obvious 404 responses.
Save a timestamped report and compare it with a second scan for changes.

steps.message: Reviewed eight source-backed candidates; selected Senro, CircleIt, and Velu because their snapshot descriptions establish concrete recurring workflows. Rejected five with thinner evidence or no autonomous loop. No existing data/posts directory or post JSON files were present to compare for duplicates.
